catalog_quote: Braun and Crofts (1965; also Crofts 1973, 1985) analyzed the language as having four opposing tone levels, three of tone and one of laryngealization (i.e. creaky voice) – accent 1 is a super-high tone, accent 2 a high level tone, accent 3 a low level tone, and accent 4 is creakiness. In this chapter (see also Picanço 1997, 2002a-c), I defend the hypothesis that the tone system of Mundurukú can be analyzed as having only two opposing levels: Low and High (hereafter L and H respectively). ... These five tonal behaviors are accounted for by assuming a four-way lexical distinction: a mora, the tone-bearing unit, may be lexically specified for H, L, or none; that is, it may be toneless (Section 8.2). Lexical H tones are stable, and lexical L tones trigger dissimilation of a following L; toneless moras get L tone by default, but this tone is inert. Unstable H tones and tonal polarity are expl…

new_statements.quote: ACENTO. Acento ocorre quase sempre na última sílaba do radical duma palavra. Quando uma palavra tem mais do que um radical, há acento em cada um. [examples: je'kõn'kõn 'comendo' — acentuados todos dois radicais (radicais duplos); jekiyjo'jõayü 'os ouvintes' (uma radical); imu'piku'pig 'queimando' (dois radicais)] [...] TOM. Há quatro tons em mundurukú. Cada vogal tem um tom "significante". [...] Os quatro tons são relativos, não absolutos. [...] Tom 1, o mais alto, é raro, ocorrendo somente em palavras ou partículas que têm o sentido de 'muito', ou qualquer sentido de superlativo [...] O quarto tom é laringalização.
new_statements.translation: STRESS. Stress occurs almost always on the last syllable of the root of a word. When a word has more than one root, there is stress on each one. [examples: 'eating' — both roots stressed (double roots); 'the listeners' (one root); 'burning' (two roots)] [...] TONE. There are four tones in Mundurukú. Each vowel has a 'significant' tone. [...] The four tones are relative, not absolute. [...] Tone 1, the highest, is rare, occurring only in words or particles that mean 'very' or have any superlative sense [...] The fourth tone is laryngealization.
new_statements.citation: Crofts, Marjorie (2004). Aspectos da Língua Munduruku. 2a ed. Cuiabá: Sociedade Internacional de Lingüística. xxii+305 pp.
new_statements.locator: Read the 1985 FIRST edition (Brasília: SIL; etnolinguistica labels the file 1981), not the listed 2004 2nd ed.: SIL record 2754 (the listed URL) is the 1985 ed. marked 'Not Available Online', and the 2004 ed.'s PDF (record 17033) could not be reached by automated download on both attempts. Quotes from the 'Chave de pronúncia': sections ACENTO and TOM, printed p. xv (PDF page 10, right half; two book pages per PDF page); particle-tone rule p. xvii (PDF page 11). scanned spacing/diacritics lightly normalized (e.g. 'quãse'->'quase', 'urna'->'uma').
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.relation_note: The catalog record (built 2026-09-12 from Picanço 2005) exits as tonal-OR-pitch accent with no stress rule; Crofts (1985 ed.) keeps the language tonal (four 'tons', with laryngealization as tone 4) and ADDS an explicit word-stress statement: root-final, one stress per root. Compatible with the catalog, adds the stress placement. Caveat: this is the first edition, not the listed 2004 second edition; the 2004 text was not obtained.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Mundurukú is described as having four lexically significant tones on every vowel (1 super-high/emphatic, 2 high, 3 low, 4 laryngealized), and in addition word stress that falls (almost always) on the final syllable of the root; a word containing two roots (reduplicated or compound stems) carries a stress on each root. Stress is thus positional within the morphological root, not the phonological word.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed as such; multi-root words are said to bear a stress on each root (three examples given), which functions like a second stress per root.
new_statements.exceptions: 'quase sempre' (almost always) root-final — exceptions are implied but none are listed. Tone, not stress, is the contrastive feature ('Há muitos pares de palavras que variam somente em tom', p. xvi); relational words and particles (be, dag, gu, ma, juy) alternate between tone 2 and tone 3 by polarity with the preceding tone (p. xvii); tone 2/3 may rise to tone 1 for emphasis or sentence intonation.
new_statements.identity_note: Crofts's grammar was written from sixteen years of fieldwork in the Cururu river villages (Santa Maria, Posto Indígena Mundurukú, Missão São Francisco; acknowledgments p. i), i.e. the Tapajós/Cururu (Pará) variety. Picanço 2005 covers the same main Mundurukú language (dissertation does not, in the sections read, single out a dialect). The Madeira (Amazonas) variety is described separately by Santos 2013, which is held by the project in the same check folder but was not among the listed works.

new_statements.quote: [§8.1, p. 310] Braun and Crofts (1965; also Crofts 1973, 1985) analyzed the language as having four opposing tone levels, three of tone and one of laryngealization (i.e. creaky voice) – accent 1 is a super-high tone, accent 2 a high level tone, accent 3 a low level tone, and accent 4 is creakiness. In this chapter (see also Picanço 1997, 2002a-c), I defend the hypothesis that the tone system of Mundurukú can be analyzed as having only two opposing levels: Low and High [...] [§8.2, p. 311] Mundurukú is a tonal language; that is, it makes use of pitch variations to lexically differentiate items. new_statements.rule_in_words: Mundurukú is a lexical tone language with two contrastive levels (H vs L) on the mora as tone-bearing unit (moras lexically H, L, toneless, or carrying a floating H; L-dissimilation, tonal polarity), creaky voice being a vowel feature that co-occurs with L tone; Braun & Crofts's super-high 'accent 1' is reanalysed as a non-contrastive intonational/boundary or emphatic tone (fn. 1, p. 310). No word-stress rule is stated anywhere; the only mention of stress is that the stressed vowel of Portuguese loanwords is mapped to an H-tone vowel.
new_statements.exceptions: Not applicable (no stress rule). Tonal exceptions handled by the four-way lexical specification; 'accent 1' excluded from the contrastive system.
new_statements.identity_note: Crofts's grammar was written from sixteen years of fieldwork in the Cururu river villages (Santa Maria, Posto Indígena Mundurukú, Missão São Francisco; acknowledgments p. i), i.e. the Tapajós/Cururu (Pará) variety. Picanço 2005 covers the same main Mundurukú language (dissertation does not, in the sections read, single out a dialect). The Madeira (Amazonas) variety is described separately by Santos 2013, which is held by the project in the same check folder but was not among the listed works.

readall_conflicts: No direct contradiction on stress, but the two sources that speak to prosody differ in framing. Crofts (1985 ed. of Aspectos, pedagogical grammar, p. xv) describes four lexically significant tones on every vowel (tone 1 super-high/emphatic, 2 high, 3 low, 4 laryngealization) AND a separate word-stress statement: stress almost always on the last syllable of the root, one stress per root in multi-root words. Picanço 2005/2007 (full phonological study) reanalyses the tone system as two levels H/L on the mora with creaky voice as a vowel feature and treats the super-high 'accent 1' as a non-contrastive intonational/emphatic tone (p. 310 fn. 1, p. 311), and never states any word-stress rule; its single mention of stress is that Portuguese loanword stress maps to H tone (p. 120). So Picanço is silent rather than contradictory on stress; Crofts's four-tone inventory versus Picanço's two-level analysis is a difference of analysis of the same pitch facts (Picanço explicitly reports and reanalyses Braun & Crofts / Crofts 1973, 1985). The catalog's existing exit (tonal, no stress rule) stands; Crofts adds a root-final stress statement that the catalog does not yet record. Sheffler's hortatory-discourse paper is silent; Crofts 1973 and Sheffler 1978 could not be opened.

audit.quote_check: confirmed in the copy we hold
audit.reasoning: Quote check: all deciding passages are verbatim in the Picanço 2005 text we hold at the stated sections and pages (8.1 p. 310 / PDF 324; 8.2 p. 311 / PDF 325; 4.4.2 PDF 134). Deciding source is a 410-pp phonology dissertation with instrumental tone data by the language's main phonologist, the best available and the work every later description defers to. Three open later sources downloaded now (Picanço 2012 teaching monograph pp. 35-36; Santos 2013 UnB MA p. 107; Gomes 2006 UnB PhD pp. 8-9) all state Mundurukú is tonal with two contrastive tones (H/L), laryngealized vowels L-only, and none describes word stress; 'acento' appears only as diacritic names or a generic clitic definition. Web search found no stress/rhythm study or JIPA illustration for Mundurukú. Coding 'tonal', domain not stated by the source, no stress rule, stands. Remaining unheld items (Braun & Crofts 1965 on JSTOR; Crofts 2004 SIL pedagogica

sources.citation: Picanço, Gessiane Lobato (2012). Introdução ao Mundurukú: fonética, fonologia e ortografia. Cadernos de Etnolingüística, Série Monografias 3. 74 pp.
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'O Mundurukú é uma língua tonal (Braun & Crofts 1965; Picanço 2002, 2005)... A língua possui dois tons contrastivos: o tom Alto (A)... e o tom Baixo (B)... Os únicos segmentos que podem carregar o tom em Mundurukú são as vogais... A forma como os tons A e B serão combinados em uma sequência é imprevisível' (all 4 disyllabic and all 8 trisyllabic H/L patterns attested; laryngealized vowels only L). No word stress/acento de intensidade is described anywhere in the monograph ('acento' occurs only as 'acento agudo/grave' = diacritics).
